newsitem.title: CHINA: China mulls Pyongyang defector, N.Koreans in vigil.
newsitem.headline: China mulls Pyongyang defector, N.Koreans in vigil.

text.p: The highest-ranking North Korean to betray his Stalinist homeland spent his fourth day marooned in a South Korean embassy office in Beijing on Saturday while China agonised over what to do with him.

Analysts said Beijing was unlikely to give in to the request for asylum in Seoul made by top Pyongyang ideologue Hwang Jang-yop until after North Korea celebrates the 55th birthday of its top leader, Kim Jong-il, on Sunday.

Hwang, ranked 24th in Pyongyangs hierarchy and a senior aide to Kim Jong-il, has become the focus of a Cold War tussle between the two Koreas, arch-enemies since their 1950-53 war ended only in a truce.
China played for time as it agonised over a diplomatic quandary -- how to usher Hwang out of Beijing without offending its old socialist comrade or its new capitalist friend.
Hwang, the scholarly architect of North Koreas national ideology of Juche, or self-reliance, was reported to be adamant he wanted to go to South Korea -- and nowhere else.
"I will die here if my determination to go to South Korea cannot be realised," Hwang said in a statement released by Seoul authorities.
"Hes very well, hes still in there and hes determined to go to (South) Korea," one South Korean embassy official said.
Hwangs fate depends on Beijing, which has signalled its annoyance with South Koreas loudhailer diplomacy, and has appealed for calm while it investigates.

South Korea appeared to fall in with Beijings approach after a meeting between its Foreign Minister Yoo Chong-ha and his Chinese counterpart Qian Qichen in Singapore on Friday failed to break the deadlock.
"I think we have started a good discussion with China and we have to wait and see," Yoo said in Singapore on Saturday. "I dont think that its right now to make any judgment on this."
China has appealed for calm and warned that it may take some time to decide what to do with Hwang. Diplomats said China may have little choice but to follow Hwangs wishes.

Dozens of North Korean diplomats and students holding vigil at the edge of a Chinese police cordon around the Seoul mission in Beijing said they were convinced Hwang had been kidnapped and wanted to hear him speak for himself.
"He is a very important person in our country," said one North Korean student among a group who said they had been told by the embassy to stake out the heavily-guarded mission.
"I want to know what happened," he said. "I am waiting for him to make an explanation.
"We just want a chance to see him," he said, denying that the North Koreans would use violent action to recover Hwang.

Police patrolling the sedate, tree-lined streets in the diplomatic district around the mission appeared ready for any possible incident, deploying a bullet-proof car at the door of the mission and bringing in a water-cannon truck.
After North Korean diplomatic cars drove right up to police barricades on Friday night, police laid spikes across approaches to the building.
Seoul sees the highest-level defection from the North as a major coup that could produce a treasure trove of intelligence on a secretive government it fears is plotting its destruction.

It is a slap in the face for Pyongyangs Kim Jong-il, whose birthday party on Sunday was intended to smooth the way for his formal accession to the posts of state president and general secretary of the ruling Workers Party.
